L0@P0: Counting preimages of homogeneous
L1@P0: configurations in 1-dimensional cellular automata
L2@P0: EDWARD J. POWLEY?, SUSAN STEPNEY
L3@P0: Department of Computer Science, University of York, UK
L4@P0: A cellular automaton (CA) is in a homogeneous configuration if
L5@P0: every cell has the same state. The preimages of a configuration
L6@P0: s are those configurations which evolve to s within a single time
L7@P0: step.
L8@P0: We present two methods of finding the total number of preimages
L9@P0: for a given homogeneous configuration. The first is more intuitive, and gives a clear picture of how the number of preimages
L10@P0: varies with the number of cells on which the CA operates, but it
L11@P0: is only workable for elementary CAs (1-dimensional binary state
L12@P0: CAs with neighbourhood size 3). The second method, based on
L13@P0: de Bruijn matrices, is more abstract, but more readily extends to
L14@P0: general 1-dimensional CAs.
L15@P0: Key words: Homogeneity, preimages, de Bruijn graphs, de Bruijn matrices, spectral graph theory
L16@P0: 1 INTRODUCTION
L17@P0: A cellular automaton (CA) is a dynamical system, discrete and uniform in
L18@P0: space and time. A CA is composed of a number of sites (cells), each of which
L19@P0: is assigned one of a finite set of states. An assignment of states to cells is a
L20@P0: configuration of the CA, and is analogous to what is usually called the “state”
L21@P0: of a dynamical system. The dynamics of the CA is defined by the local update
L22@P0: rule, a function mapping the “current” state of a cell and its neighbours to the
L23@P0: ? email: ed@cs.york.ac.uk
L24@P0-1: 1“next” state of that cell. The local update rule extends to the global map, a
L25@P1: function mapping the “current” configuration to the “next” configuration, in
L26@P1: the natural way.
L27@P1: In general, the global map is not bijective, so strictly speaking it has no
L28@P1: inverse. However, it is often useful to find the preimages of a given configuration; that is, those configurations which the global map sends to the given
L29@P1: configuration. Intuitively, if the configuration at time t is known, then the
L30@P1: preimages of that configuration are the possible configurations at time t − 1.
L31@P1: Wuensche and Lesser [13] give an efficient algorithm for finding preimages.
L32@P1: One way of visualising the dynamics of a CA is by drawing a transition
L33@P1: graph (or transition diagram). This is a directed graph whose vertices represent the configurations of the CA, and whose edges represent the transitions
L34@P1: between configurations according to the global map. The in-degree of a vertex in the transition graph is precisely the number of preimages for the corresponding configuration, and so numbers of preimages are a measure of the
L35@P1: “branchiness” of the graph.
L36@P1: In [7], we study symmetries (formally, automorphisms or self-isomorphisms)
L37@P1: of transition graphs. By studying how the number of symmetries varies with
L38@P1: the number of cells, we obtain a partial classification of the elementary CAs
L39@P1: (1-dimensional, binary state CAs with neighbourhood size 3).
L40@P1: In [8], we specialise our results to linear CAs: CAs whose local rules
L41@P1: (and thus global maps) are linear functions. We derive an expression for the
L42@P1: number of automorphisms of the transition graph for a linear CA, and one of
L43@P1: the terms in this expression is the number of preimages for the homogeneous
L44@P1: configuration of zeroes.
L45@P1: In this paper, we discuss how to find the numbers of preimages of homogeneous configurations. Even though linear CAs motivate us to carry out this
L46@P1: work, the results are equally applicable to nonlinear CAs. After introducing
L47@P1: the necessary definitions in Section 2, we describe two different approaches
L48@P1: to counting preimages.
L49@P1: The first approach (Section 3) works by considering the possible lengths
L50@P1: of sequences of consecutive cells in the same state. When the number of
L51@P1: preimages is considered as a function of the number of cells, we see three
L52@P1: distinct types of behaviour: constancy, periodicity, and exponential growth.
L53@P1: The string length approach gives an intuitive understanding of when and why
L54@P1: these behaviours arise.
L55@P1: The second approach (Section 4) applies results from spectral graph theory
L56@P1: to the de Bruijn graphs of the CA. Specifically, we consider the eigenvalues
L57@P1: of the adjacency matrices of the de Bruijn graphs (these adjacency matrices
L58@P1-2: 2are known as de Bruijn matrices). While this method is not quite as intuitive
L59@P2: as considering string lengths, it is far more useful for producing numerical
L60@P2: results. In Section 4.3, we show that this approach can also be applied to
L61@P2: configurations which are heterogeneous but periodic.
L62@P2: 2 DEFINITIONS AND NOTATION
L63@P2: Consider a 1-dimensional CA with state set Σ, neighbourhood radius r and
L64@P2: local rule f : Σ2r+1 → Σ, operating on a lattice of N cells. In this paper we
L65@P2: consider lattices with periodic boundary condition, where the leftmost cell is
L66@P2: considered to be adjacent to the rightmost, so that the cells are indexed by
L67@P2: the elements of ZN (the integers modulo N). This is not the only choice of
L68@P2: boundary condition, but the alternatives (treating the boundary cells differently to the rest, or allowing the lattice to be unbounded so that the effective
L69@P2: number of cells is infinite) present obvious practical problems.
L70@P2: A configuration of this CA is a mapping from ZN to Σ. We will write such
L71@P2: a configuration as a string over Σ of length N, and write Σ
L72@P2: N for the set of all
L73@P2: configurations. A homogeneous configuration in which each cell has state q

L76@P2: The local rule f extends to the global map F : ΣN → Σ
L77@P2: N . The preimages of a configuration u are those configurations v such that F(v) = u. The
L78@P2: successor of u is the configuration F(u). Note that CAs are deterministic
L79@P2: (every configuration has precisely one successor), but not necessarily surjective or injective (a configuration may have zero, one, or many preimages). If
L80@P2: a configuration has at least one preimage, it is said to be reachable; an unreachable configuration (one with no preimages) is often called a Garden of
L81@P2: Eden configuration.
L82@P2: A cyclic shift is a transformation which shifts the entire configuration by
L83@P2: a certain number of cells, respecting the periodic boundary condition of the
L84@P2: lattice. For example, applying a cyclic shift to the right by one cell to the
L85@P2: configuration
L86@P2: x0x1 . . . xN−2xN−1 (1)
L87@P2: yields the configuration
L88@P2: xN−1x0 . . . xN−3xN−2 . (2)
L89@P2: Cyclic shifts are “symmetries” of any CA, in the sense that shifting a configuration cyclically and then applying the CA’s global map to the result is
L90@P2: equivalent to applying the global map first and shifting the result.
